title: Perforated Peptic Ulcer
summary: Site, free-gas traps, first vs best test, resuscitate before theatre, and the omental patch.
closing: Front wall perforates, back wall bleeds; first film is erect, best film is CT; resuscitate, then patch.

objectives.text: Choose the commonest perforation site and pair anterior vs posterior duodenal wall with perforation vs bleeding (and the artery eroded)
Name the commonest cause of pneumoperitoneum, and tell true free gas from Chilaiditi pseudo-pneumoperitoneum using the signs
Recognise the classic presentation and the three stages, picking the false-calm reaction stage and the appendicitis mimic as traps
Pick the first investigation versus the most sensitive one, and state what PYQ keys expected versus current practice
Decide what a clear erect film, or a soft abdomen in an elderly or steroid-treated patient, does and does not exclude
Choose the right view for a patient who cannot sit up and the right contrast (and the contraindicated one)
Pick the first step in a shocked patient with peritonitis: resuscitation, antibiotics and PPI before theatre
Choose the operation of choice and name the patch correctly (Graham versus Cellan-Jones)
Choose post-repair care and the gastric-ulcer addition, rejecting routine vagotomy or gastrectomy
Decide when Taylor non-operative management is acceptable and what it is called
State the Boey score components and what raises mortality
Tell look-alike eponyms and risk factors apart (Curling vs Cushing, Kehr vs shoulder-tip, NSAID, steroid, cocaine)

traps.trap: Posterior duodenal wall or lesser curvature is the commonest perforation site; posterior DU perforates (merged with TR2: wrong artery for the posterior DU bleed)
Pneumoperitoneum is always caused by a perforated peptic ulcer
Any gas under the right dome of the diaphragm is free intraperitoneal gas
CT is the first investigation, or erect X-ray is the most sensitive test
PYQ key and current practice give the same answer for investigation of choice
A normal erect chest X-ray excludes perforation
When the patient cannot sit up, a supine or right-sided view shows free gas
Free gas rises immediately, so the erect film can be taken at once
Surgery comes first in a shocked peritonitis patient; resuscitation and antibiotics wait
Non-operative (Taylor) management suits any stable or diagnosed perforation
The PYQ-key operation name and the strictly correct name are the same
Vagotomy with drainage or partial gastrectomy is the standard operation for perforated duodenal ulcer
Curling's ulcer follows head injury and Cushing's ulcer follows burns
Shoulder-tip pain or tracked fluid is linked to the wrong eponym
The period of reaction means the patient is recovering
A patient who lies still has colic and one who writhes has peritonitis
A perforated gastric ulcer is closed like a duodenal ulcer with no biopsy
Barium is the best contrast study for a suspected or sealed perforation
The Boey score includes age, perforation size or bleeding, with delay 12 hours and shock below 90 (merged with TR22: Boey thresholds)
No board-like rigidity in an elderly or steroid-treated patient rules out perforation
